source.title: From predictions to confidence intervals: an empirical study of conformal prediction methods for in-context learning
source.authors: Zhen Huang; Simone Rossi; Rui Yuan; T. Hannagan

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses Kaplan and Hoffmann scaling-law analyses as a methodology, but its scaling experiment models the quality of conformal prediction intervals for synthetic in-context regression—not held-out language-model cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The reported scaling result concerns predictive-interval quality, a different target from the loss in the claim. The paper also reports coverage, Wasserstein-distance, and runtime results, but those do not measure the claim versions. Cited scaling-law results are not treated as findings of this study.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the Hoffmann et al. parametric form and fitting procedure but fits it to conformal-interval quality. Figure 6's y-axis is the Wasserstein distance between CP-with-ICL and ridge-oracle typicalness distributions. The models are tiny linear-self-attention models on synthetic linear regression. No held-out pretraining loss, language-model or otherwise, is scaled. The result measures a different construct, so it is recorded under fits_no_version, not as a test of V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude the fitted law is a good proxy for the quality of conformal predictive intervals, judged from two frontier-allocated runs. They find the optimal model size scales faster than data, which 'slightly contradicts' Hoffmann et al. They hypothesize this is because they evaluate interval quality rather than perplexity. They suggest larger-capacity models are more beneficial for uncertainty quantification, possibly linked to 'uncertainty collapse'.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts a scaling-law parameterization and compute-allocation analysis to conformal-prediction interval quality in synthetic linear regression, rather than measuring language-model held-out cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors attribute the different compute-optimal allocation from Hoffmann et al. to evaluating predictive-interval quality rather than language-model perplexity.

fits_no_version.finding: A Chinchilla-form law was fit to 40 linear-self-attention models at 3e11 and 1e12 FLOPs. The target was the Wasserstein distance between CP-with-ICL and ridge-oracle typicalness. It gives a=0.62, b=0.38 (N grows faster than D). Two runs at the predicted allocation for 3e12 and 1e13 FLOPs lie 'close to the predicted frontier'. No fit error or uncertainty is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Uncertainty-quantification quality of in-context conformal prediction follows a Chinchilla-form law in N and D. Its compute-optimal allocation favours model size over data.

record.peer_reviewed: Symposium on Advances in Approximate Bayesian Inference
record.problems: The scaling experiment uses synthetic linear-regression tasks and a simplified linear-self-attention model. The paper reports no uncertainty estimate for the fitted scaling exponents; its reported scaling target is not language-model pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for the claim were left out; other reported results concern coverage, predictive-distribution distances, or runtime rather than the claim's loss-scaling versions.

untested.parts: Power-law decline of held-out pretraining loss in N, D or C; the study never reports its pretraining MSE versus scale.
Extrapolation of loss fits. The study's two 3e12/1e13 FLOP runs check a fit of a non-loss metric, only about 1 order of magnitude beyond the fit budgets.
Compute-optimal allocation for pretraining loss. The a=0.62, b=0.38 split is for Wasserstein distance.
Effect of shape at fixed parameter count; not studied.
Power-law loss in other regimes. A synthetic-regression pretraining loss scaling was not measured.
Downstream predictability from scale or loss; not studied as such.
Dependence of loss exponents on setup or fitting choices. The authors attribute their differing split to a different target metric but test no fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's main contributions are coverage, Wasserstein-distance, runtime and distribution-shift results for CP with ICL; none bear on the claim. The scaling section is a small adaptation exercise: tiny models, a narrow compute range, and no reported fit quality. Even read loosely as V5 or V2 evidence, it would be very weak, because the target is not a training loss.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether small-run fits predict held-out language-model loss on much larger runs.
The loss-minimising parameter/token allocation for language-model pretraining loss.
Effects of architecture details at fixed parameter count on language-model loss.
Whether the same scaling law for pretraining loss holds in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream-task performance scaling or its relation to pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model pretraining-loss exponents and compute-optimal allocation on setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: 40 models (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: Pre-trained linear-self-attention models on synthetic linear-regression tasks
rows.operation_detail: Fit a scaling function for conformal-prediction interval quality versus model parameters and training data, then estimate compute-optimal allocation.

conditions.value: Quality of conformal prediction intervals; not held-out language-model cross-entropy
Chinchilla package; L-BFGS; asymmetric MAE with λ = 0.1

rows.measure: Estimated compute-optimal scaling exponents for model parameters and data points; reported proximity of two trained allocations to the predicted frontier.
rows.value: a = 0.62 and b = 0.38; the two models trained with compute-efficient allocations of 3e12 and 1e13 FLOPs are described as close to the predicted frontier.
rows.note: Aggregate scaling-fit result over 40 models; the paper says this allocation makes model size scale faster than data and slightly contradicts Hoffmann et al. It concerns interval quality, so it does not establish any listed version of the language-model loss claim.
rows.check: The link to none is correct. The measure should say the fitted target is the Wasserstein distance shown on Fig. 6's y-axis, not generic 'interval quality'. Appendix C.2 says 'loss Li', which is ambiguous. The scaling target is not pretraining MSE loss, and no goodness-of-fit is reported. The model size range spans about 1e4–1e5 parameters per the Fig. 6 axis; it is not 'not stated'.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
